items.album: V/A :: soak vol 2 (Soak)
items.excerpt: soak vol 2 unfolds like a damaged transmission from somewhere intimate and unplaceable—32 fractured, emotional, and strangely beautiful pieces stitched together from the outer edges of contemporary electronic sound. items.body: soak vol 2 unfolds like a damaged transmission from somewhere intimate and unplaceable—32 fractured, emotional, and strangely beautiful pieces stitched together from the outer edges of contemporary electronic sound. An international community focused on contemporary sound soak vol 2 by soak   Angular and granular electronica with some minor guitarica. There is probably no dancing and definitely no sleeping, this is all art—so rejoice! 32 very strange episodes, plenty to baffle the listener. Soak (the record label) is based in Petropavl, Kazakhstan. Soak 2 is a second compilation album by that label, an international community focused on contemporary sound as a means of emotional liberation & self-inquiry, featuring various kinds of music, ranging from lamebient & downtempo to quirky sound-design, raw sonic intimacy & processed emo, whatever that may be. “This is something we are proud to share, aiming at fostering a sense of unity, artistic freedom & love.“ The project was gathered and meticulously curated throughout 2025. “We hadn’t planned it to turn out that long, 32 tracks crept up like an uncontrolled desire of getting tattooed over and over again. As a result, ‘soak body’ is etched with a (s)extensive selection of self-recognition-evoking music by sound producers & musicians across the globe. Raw or refined, recorded live, carefully produced, (un)processed or playfully generated, the diversity of sound and approach eventually point at something intimate: the ‘how to be’. A shared ‘something’ we truly celebrate together via media at hand.”​ A part of proceeds will go to Isaakov dog shelter in Petropavl, Kazakhstan. The artists heard on this anthology are: s[].any, goo, lycopsid_,  OL,  sidechain unit, tumy, free version, other joe, louis vogue,  яома bantik ³³³,  obe,  s.drift,  double blind,  Alien Recycling,  obi uto,  moemu, zuno,  Infant,  Kilou,  virtual echo,  DJ Birdbath,  kk.Shucko,  marat koshkin,  Yerofeyev,  16:9 ratio,  duun,  ebilen, inferior design,  Alien Team,  slyn, poole,  bad lsd trips,  defkon, and Sta Dormida. Curated by a b, marat koshkin & a. doina, Mostly mastered by yeyo & a b. Artwork by marat koshkin & a. doina. Merch design by marat koshkin. One of the best aspects of anthologies is that smaller projects have the opportunity to exhibit in a common showcase, reaching more of the whole community, to expose their work and to experience the reactions. None of the tracks are very long, the shortest one is less than one minute. If something puts you off, hang on, there will be something new coming along soon, or maybe more of the same but somehow different. Some aspects are similar, but each track stands alone. The names are creative, to decode this, here you will find the moniker of the creating entity, a hyphen, followed by the track title and the length in minutes, and a brief description of what I think that I heard. 1. s[].any – t.here 05:55 — Opens into a dark mood, I imagine that I hear many voices hidden in the mix, which is a sound collage, with different surprises. Our dreamy poetic singer is honest, the overall sound has lots of little flavors in a delicious complex collage stew. So strange. 2. goo – Secret 03:37 — A classical guitar, with some electronics whirled about, a cello, a singer, a robot plumber. Fragments of voices that echo amidst the tunneling strings and things. Easy drifting instrumentals with strange effects and odd bits here and there. 3. lycopsid_ – raupe 03:40 — “Lycopsid” is a botanical term for clubmosses, and Lycopsid (or lycopsid) is a Leipzig, Germany-based musical artist, known for producing electronic or ambient music, with tracks available on platforms like Bandcamp and Pandora. The sound here is celestial, a steady awakening into increasing brightness with interesting sound collages or wet chattering bits sprinkled and patterned about. 4. OL – Softshell 02:08 — The collected cadence is a bit loose, mumbling taps and tings, shuffling percussive snaps and shudders. It lunges forward, it pauses and holds, it shifts and prepares to lunge, it starts again. I can dig it. It whispers to me about beats while staying fluid and just flowing with sticky stop-start moments built in. 5. sidechain unit – wasted youth riddim 03:32 — I think there are voices, fragments including screaming happy kids in a playground hidden within the mix, which comes up harsh and stays very interesting, percussive clacks, perhaps some island riddim, there are ghosts flicker dancing, and a roller coaster where they all scream together. The beat is skeletal, with an odd missing beat pattern and new mumbling taps and tings, shuffling percussive snaps and shudders. 6. tumy – frostlings 03:48 — A dusty ghost piano melody loop and an agitated electronic spirit bouncing about, echo effects gone wild, in a deep dub style. There are many things going on at once, the piano, and percussive elements that echo and shatter, about half way through the strange beat gets stronger. The piano stays perfectly on course. 7. free version – moonlight yuh spotlight yuh 06:05 — Somewhere in the abandoned old factory ruins by the sea, in a big dark cave there are strange radios playing, or maybe poetic people reciting lines, or both and more. This sounds like it is probably dangerous, voices are talking and there are echoes, plenty of water. I do not understand any words, which are mostly repetitive. There are large monsters moving about off in the distance, I hear some smoothly running machine noises and banging about. And more water. 8. other joe – every image (ft. concave reflection) 04:28 — A piano, people breathing, someone is talking, there is some kind of electronic instrument, nice and slow. Mystery at every moment, dripping water, maybe a flute, odd woodwinds, slow and quiet and cautious, full of microscopic details. Spraying water? The piano keeps dreaming and seems distant sometimes. The bowed drones have the sky here. 9. louis vogue – out of reach (ft. saga charlotte) 00:59 — Louis Vogue is an electronic music artist, DJ, and co-founder of the Brussels-based collective and event series Club Détour, known for playing atmospheric and experimental sets on Kiosk Radio. The short dreamy misty track bursts in, I hear drama, sadness and darkness on a sweeping scale, singing over the storm of glitchy-pitched musical tones. 10. яома bantik ³³³ – ₉⁹₉ (yeyo & a b edit) 02:16 — ЯOMA BANTIK @romabantik is a Russian artist from the Urals, working with metal, natural and industrial heritages. I hear a fella and his guitar, strummin’ and singin’, sounds great to me. Good times, with no serious fancy science fiction studio effects. A young man alone, telling his heart. 11. obe – iji’s dub 06:37 — I think this one feels like we are deep underwater, the throbbing reverb feels like a dub mix, with various bouncing pulse echoes, the playful living echo vibration creature crawls about above the constant pulse flowing inward slowly then flowing outward, repeating, like breathing in your sleep. The dark water flows for miles below us. There are UFOs down there too. 12. s.drift – quatro CD 03:50 — Nervous  and clicky like a rhythm, or maybe more like a collage, with odd forward and backward sounds, blending into a lighter abstract clicky beat, maybe adding a hi hat cymbal effect, an unexpected voice beep pops by a few times, while the shadows shake and shimmy. A drum set somehow shows up. We step forth with pep. 13. double blind – fade 02:29 — Water flowing, strange environmental humming rings, with mysterious winds and rain. The voice sounds drained and perhaps coming from another world. The message is in the form of hopeful poetry, and is not obvious. In my mind’s eye I see candles in the misty rings. 14. Alien Recycling – Pareidolia Cat Dub 03:44 — I am always trying to find meaningful faces or messages in musical clouds or in chaos. Here is an electronic cat that slides. There is an echo rhythm beat, drawing some space night ramblers. The beat is not steady and nearly seems to fall apart, and rallies a few times then eases off. I have been feeding that cat. 15. obi uto – oysq 03:33 — Perhaps this is just how they talk, strange beeps and clicking-rushing tones. No beats, no words, plenty of odd looping collage fragmentations, pulling from a unique musique concrete style and beyond. The feeling is restless. 16. moemu, zuno – petal traces 04:47 — Moemu and zuno are two musical artists associated with ambient, electronic, chill-out music contexts or lo-fi soundscapes, often featured in mix sets, and are found on Pandora and Bandcamp. I hear fragments of so many things, dark loop dreams that make no sense but are restful, pouring spilling cascading repeating flowing falling scattering evaporating, restless and gently convulsive, chaotic, there are void ghosts and melancholia floods over the roller coasters. I try to get there early and stay late. 17. Infant – jewel 03:01 — From twitchy robot bleeps to greebles rumbling, coming through a small tube with some shortwave radio throbbing and ringing, or maybe they are simply talking amongst themselves. There are  little spinning bumping bells and a tap-ring collage. A beat comes about, explodes and gets wild, smooths and bumps along, the flow always gets busy in places after the extended coasting interludes. soak vol 2 by Kilou   18. Kilou – Blurry 03:40 — Somewhere deep in space we float upside down, feet over eyebrows, there is buzzing and a musical instrument strumming lightly. Some guy is singing while the dragons and other monsters size the room. Soon chains are broken. A guy is talking and singing, playing a guitar, flying feathered electronic snakes swirling about, seeking a hole in outer space. I hear strumming, spare shovels and  tapping glasses with ice. I didn’t tell you everything. 19. virtual echo – j trip 04:35 — In the wash water, jiggling as the machine works, the sloshing water sets the beat. I hear nifty chattering little rhythms and throbbing waves of activities, her voices echo, skyrockets splash, there may be a drum kit, and now we are cooking, throbbing right along. This is where I belong. 20. DJ Birdbath – Rose Drip 04:06 — DJ Birdbath is the artist name for Ian Baxter, an electronic music producer based in the South Island of New Zealand, known for ambient and experimental music, often featuring deconstructed sounds, fragmented rhythms, and shoegaze-tinged vocals influenced by his past, often using a mix of real and generated samples. His music is featured on NTS Radio, SoundCloud, and Bandcamp. He released the album Memory Empathy (2024) via Theory Therapy, which features a blend of samples and influences from his time in the UK. The sound here is an abstract beat pattern that never stops changing, loops with flowing chaos and surprises, mostly variations on the instrumental constructions. Somewhere about half way in, they settle into a very catchy complex groove that stays uncertain but keeps going. They fly off, they fade. 21. kk.Shucko – another missed mirage 03:26 — kk.Shucko is an San Francisco-based experimental club producer and DJ known for crafting intricate, high-res techno, IDM, and warped drum and bass soundscapes, her sets revel in composing evenings that sew together soft and hard, continuity and catharsis draw listeners into an alien realm, and fuses needy rhythms, ambient, and club music to create immersive, imagined biomes. Associated with Club Moniker and Ommaya Records, they create “hyperspace” audio, often incorporating elements like glass and gel, and hold a residency at SutroFM. I hear energized chattering electronic squirrels, also scratchy electronified voices painted on the air. The squirrels keep me busy, some of the sound is harsh with whispers hidden inside, hit with sharp short and zappy bolts, melting into a bubbling sea of writhing monsters and phantoms. Darned cool. 22. marat koshkin – cry OS 03:37 — Marat Koshkin is a musician and artist from Petropavlovsk, Kazakhstan, recently located in Saint-Petersburg. The beat is catchy from the jump, splashy weaving beats stay strong and powerful mixed with the collage nicely, gettin’ jammy with multiple instruments, gettin’ down within the change and solids. A winsome laugh has been captured. 23. Yerofeyev – Smares (Senglar Rmx) 05:52 — Senglar is an electronic music artist and composer known for producing experimental, atmospheric, immersive, often dark, and downtempo electronic soundscapes. Based on recent music releases, Senglar often works within the niche of electronic, ambient, and downtempo genres, featuring 2024 album releases like Sensen – Hum. A rolling ball of fragmented multisounds, shortwave abstract whispers, electronic complex and plenty to listen to per sparkle, great for head rushes and surprises. I am sure there is more to the story as to how Senglar came to remix Yerofeyev’s Smares. 24. 16:9 ratio – Nothing Drive 03:15 — 16:9 ratio is likely the moniker for Geunf, a multidisciplinary artist, DJ, and producer based in Ottawa, Canada. He is known for blending techno, pop, and deconstructed club music. He released the ambient/experimental project Our Keyboards in 2025. He is also a member of the pop trio Los3r. I hear a children’s playground and people talking just out of reach, the beat trots up and off we go with nice propulsion, dancing snowflakes, the feeling defines royal and grand (both), towards the end we are at a full gallop with happily laughing snare drums and a big wow finish. 25. duun – chill! 03:28 — A machine is dancing inside of a twisting huge towering steel monster, I sense a dark voodoo beach with a moonlight fire, the rolling beat goes on and on, the feeling is fearsome and close, I hear a sly dark dub beat, probably from a strong dancing doom machine. 26. ebilen – aeon 04:00 — Ebilen is an electronic music artist known for tracks like “Strange Emotion” and the album pihkal (Base 1), releasing music through labels like Tabula Rasa Records and featuring on SoundCloud. They produce in genres often associated with underground electronic or ambient styles. I am in outer space, no gravity, no up or down, spinning slowly, whispers always getting more complex, shifting and ticking inside the mind. Something changes, the energizing chaos dance continues while ghosts call in the dark empty corridors, tiny punchy robot construction workers appear everywhere all at once for a little while, things continue to change, finally we finish swirling with whispers and the clock ticks. 27. inferior design – conning 04:47 — Outer space has no corners or answers, aliens and robots scoot along as we explore all these little pieces, like sand only smaller and with more shapes and colors, flashing and glittering particles spreading everywhere. There is no gravity so the spinning can seem slower, granular overstimulation transports some to a new place with new possibilities. Now we are having a sunrise inside the chaos collage, shooting lasers across the tracks, as chaos echoes and bumps about. This too shall morph. 28. Alien Team – my team 03:33 — Somewhere way out there, by a waterfall, the birdbeams call as they rush by. The rumbling loop brings up the low end, the birdbeams come and go, now we have a beat rumble stomp shake throbstep march while the birdbeams swirl overhead. A continuation of rushing water, with new strange birds taking over and proliferating, growing and developing, learning to dance. Soon the tribe is grooving. Now we are at the waterfall with the chaos birds. I woke up wondering where I was. At home of course. 29. slyn, poole – arc 04:18 — Slyn, a Glasgow-based sound artist, live performer, and DJ, is known for immersive, experimental, and eccentric club sounds that blend IDM, bass, and jungle with ambient textures, heavily influenced by a background in marine biology and themes of hydrofeminism and queer ecology, with soundscapes that are often described as underwater, dreamy, or “algae-like.” I am seeking more about Poole. What I hear here is a new jungle of fabrics and textures, mysterious vocalisms, many things at once. There is a primitive beat picking up, I hear the jungle in the distance. Now and then some guitar tapping time baps along. I want to live here under the arc. 30. bad lsd trips – eno river 04:46 — bad lsd trips is a collaborative music project between artists Domingo Castillo Flores and Mónica Mesa (who performs as doris dana). Based in Miami, Florida, the duo formed during the pandemic, producing music that blends elements of early industrial, dark ambient, tape music, and drone “psychedelic meditations” and “murky field recordings” with “ASMR-adjacent synths.” My mind melts, I hear strange twisted whistles, an emerging beat like a train rattle power turnip ringing shards of metal along comes the boat, an odd motor throb whispering starshine flotters about and the motor keeps running. The individual words are lost for me, the poetic tone and vibe are clear and strong, I float off into another dream with newer words that are never easier to remember. 31. defkon – sun tunnels 03:04 — We are building a new solar passageway, and adding a piano loop skeleton with strange attachments and things to tap. The piano stays solid while the changes bring new creatures that make sound, odd new sounds, piano loops and wild improv with little hand instruments adding into the pattern. 32. Sta Dormida – Trace Abruption 04:44 — Sta Dormida is an independent musical artist, singer-songwriter, producer, and audio engineer who composes, records, produces, mixes, and masters their own music. Known for releases such as Ace of Grace (2025), More Like Never (2025), and It’s Rigged (2024), they are active on platforms like Spotify and Bandcamp. This contribution features her singing and playing classical guitar, nothing electronic, just dry fingers on strings and layered singing. I want to stay here forever. A former circus aerialist, she pioneered the male-dominated industry in the early 1900s by mastering traditional hand-poked (“stick-and-poke”) tattooing, helping to introduce tattoo artistry to inland America. soak vol 2 is available on soak. I agree with those who view Tony as a gifted virtuoso, I couldn't agree more with you all! However, his virtuosity aside, I do believe this album lacks the variety that would make this one a true valuable asset within the guitarist set of albums to listen to. Don't get me wrong, I do believe this guy was original back in 1987. But after listening to the first four songs of the album, don't you feel they could've been just one long track since they're all in the same chords? Anyhow, it was an interesting listen, and I would give other of his albums a try, sure.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Explorers Club is one of the most exciting prog supergroups of the 90s. This Magna Carta project isheaded and masterminded by Trent Gardner, keyboard player and songwriter for Magellan, who is herejoined by John Petrucci on guitars, Billy Sheehan on bass guitar, and Terry Bozzio on drums,together with four different vocalists, among which the names of James LaBrie and D. C. Cooper makea serious impression. Additionally, the supergroup's debut album features contributions from DerekSherinian (keyboards), Wayne Gardner (guitars), Steve Howe (acoustic guitar), and James Murphy(guitars). Composed by Trent Gardner, 'Age of Impact', as goes the title of this 1998 album, is abold musical odyssey that for me represents one of the most successful collaborations in modernprogressive rock. The music of Explorers Club is a daring marriage of heavy but melodic neo-prog andtechnical prog metal, featuring lost of shredding and mind-bending soloing, complex arrangements andextended instrumental sections, polyrhythms, and a few truly experimental bits.I am certain that this album was conceived as one continuous piece of music, and while the albumtrack list features five distinct compositions, the former are actually connected and flow into eachother almost seamlessly, giving the impression of one gargantuan composition that goes throughseveral distinct sections, but remains true to the main album theme. Opening track 'Fate Speaks'sits at sixteen minutes and happens to be one of the most technically intense pieces on here - fromthe complex opening section, which is all-instrumental, to the excellent verses that come in at alater point and the scorchingly rapid solos of John Petrucci (and James Murphy, supposedly), this isa really strong prog metal suite that features Bret Douglas as the lead vocalist. The sound is epic,bombastic, celebratory and straight up wild, and fans of LTE and Dream Theater should reallyappreciate this massive track. 'Fading Fast' then introduces a more ethereal, keyboard-driven soundas well as some world music influences, which are explored brilliantly by Trent Gardner. Third track'No Returning' revisits the heavier sounds from the beginning of the album, as this part of thesuite serves as an almost all-instrumental middle section with excellent guitars and keys, while thesole vocal part is sang by James LaBrie. 'Time Enough', which is the fourth song on the album,explores a melodramatic new age sound and features some thoughtful lyrics, which are sang by D. C.Cooper, while the closing piece 'Last Call', returns to the main theme and expands it beautifully,concluding the record with a flamboyant streak of guitar pyrotechnics, occupying a good chunk of the11-minute-long final composition.'Age of Impact' is a fantastic project in my view - the complexity of the compositions, thegrandiose ideas, and the excellent execution should be seen as a treat by fans of prog rock and progmetal alike. The balanced vocal work and the cohesion of the entire work are commendable, too.However, unlike LTE or Dream Theater, the music of Explorers Club manages to evoke that classic progfeeling in a beautiful way, which is why I think it is one of the most underrated heavy prog gemfrom the late 1990s.

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 970Porcupine Tree is an English progressive rock band that was formed in 1987 in Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire. Their debut album 'On The Sunday Of Life'' was released in 1991. It's a selection of compositions from earlier unofficial cassette releases. The first 'full-fledged' album of Porcupine Tree isn't only an exhibition of the young artist's most interesting ideas, not only the essence of creative work concentrated in the psychedelic convention which Wilson undertook in the second half of the 80's, but is a compelling work, by all means enigmatic, mysterious, shrouded in an aura of unreality. It collects Wilson's favourite songs from those years into a double album. Listening in retrospect, we may well find pretty nonplussed at this highly experimental mixture of psychedelic and space rock, moving from ambient flute pieces to the sort of whimsical nonsense that wouldn't be out of place on the early Pink Floyd's releases.The line up 'On The Sunday Of Life'' is composed by Steven Wilson (vocals, guitar and other instruments like keyboards and programming). 'On The Sunday Of Life'' also has the participation of some other musicians. So, we also have here the presence of Malcolm Stocks 'Solomon St. Jemain' (vocals and additional guitars), Master Timothy Masters (oboe) and John Marshall (drums), as the guest musicians of the album.'On The Sunday Of Life'' has eighteen tracks. 'Music For The Head' is very short, a kind of an introduction to the album. It has a rather sinister tone, with some nice flute work to go with it. 'Jupiter Island' is from Wilson's adolescent days. It's a charming psychedelic tune with lyrics that features some fast paced drumming, apparently from a drum machine. The next pieces are two highly experimental short pieces. 'Third Eye Surfer' is a nice dissonant song with an odd metered drum improvisation along with synths and keys. The title track is an atmospheric piece dominated by the keyboards with a lot of sounds. Both pieces form two relaxed pieces on the album. 'The Nostalgia Factory' is the second song on the album including lyrics. This is a very nice psychedelic song with a great beat where the vocals sound distinctly due to the vocoder. The next two are yet more experimental pieces with some rather sinister spoken dialog. 'Space Transmission' is mostly spoken again through a vocoder. It's a very dark and ambient track. 'Message From A Self-Destructing Turnip' is another spoken piece, a very short ambient break piece. Both are psychedelic at its extreme. 'Radioactive Toy' is an interesting psychedelic epic with nice heavy guitar melodies and slowly pounding drums. It still is one of the favourite Porcupine Tree's songs played live as an encore. It has stood up to the test of time amazingly well. 'Nine Cats' is a nice acoustic track despite being very simple. It continues to emphasize the eclectic nature of the album. It became a fan's favourite that was rarely performed live. 'Hymn' is another short instrumental that has some strange vocal sounds and synths. It's more of a soundscape interlude between songs. 'Footprints' is also from Wilson's adolescent days. It also reminds me of Pink Floyd in Syd Barrett's era. It's another song with lyrics, guitar and synths. The next two tracks continue to absorb Pink Floyd's early influences. 'Linton Samuel Dawson' is awesomely weird and frenetic but very fun too. It's based on psychedelic drums and some mind blowing strange vocals through a vocoder. 'And The Swallows Dance Above The Sun' is another semi obscure odd track with a drum machine beat combined with ambient keyboards and vocals. 'Queen Quotes Crowley' is technically an instrumental. It has many psychedelic effects with some nice guitar work and where the vocals are in the reverse. The two next tracks are the final short instrumentals of this album. 'No Luck With Rabbits' is a very short experimental instrumental of synths, a kind of a soundscape between songs. 'Begonia Seduction Scene' is a lovely instrumental with some great acoustic guitar work and synths. 'This Long Silence' is a psychedelic up-tempo song that again features vocals through a vocoder. It follows the same style as some other songs, a good indication of what is to follow. 'It Will Rain For A Million Years' is another track that points the direction that the band would later take. There are hardly any lyrics on this song. Most of it is instrumental and ambient. It features a nice guitar work supported by a heavy rhythm, a good way to close the album.Conclusion: 'On The Sunday Of Life...' although in its moments heralds the later stylistic development of the band, as a whole is rather a sign of its time, a testimony to the band's interesting genesis. However, this doesn't diminish its value. It's a unique album, an extremely eclectic work. It treats this eclecticism as a method of surrealistic expression. It has its standout tracks, mainly 'Radioactive Toy', 'Nine Cats' and 'It Will Rain For A Million Years' that are worth the price of the purchase alone, but also features plenty of filler that you'll either enjoy for what it is or skip past every time. Nonetheless, for Porcupine Tree's fans, this album is of course a must to get to know the beginnings of the band and the roots of their later works. Still, I think it can be rather misleading for those who want to get to know the band. Anyhow and despite 'On The Sunday Of Life...' isn't as mature as later Porcupine Tree's stuff it still is recommendable.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.body: Review by alainPP — BRUCE SOORD's 5th album, recorded over 10 years ago, exudes a heightened dreamlike atmosphere, based on acoustic sounds, reflecting his past life like a musical epitaph."Concepcion" opens with an acoustic guitar riff, a melancholic Southern lament, an evening in Chile, a heartfelt cry for his mother giving birth. "Meet Me on the Downs" is a mid-tempo ballad with his voice as the instrument, a slow, ethereal, decrescendoing sound reminiscent of the end of a concert in Hamburg. "Pillars," with its melody etched into our musical subconscious, features a slide guitar that shines, illuminates, and opens the mind. It evokes the feeling of a Western ballad, riding these reverberating notes, rich like a cactus at sunset, where the heat makes the air vibrate. A beautiful melody dealing with excessive introspection, the quest for balance, a reference to Saint Simeon Stylite. "You Made a Promise," with its prominent, almost oppressive acoustic guitar over a pastoral choir, and a raw, crystalline vocal delivery, all in under three minutes. "Our Predicament" features lingering guitar notes and metronomic sixteenth notes amplifying the contemplative sound. The off-kilter vocals heighten the impression of a solitary lament. The electric guitar solo evokes the plaintive post-rock of KWOON, an intimate moment you wouldn't want to share with your horse at dusk. "Day of Wrath" shifts gears, repetitive from the start, reminiscent of Mariusz's work on LUNATIC SOUL. A catchy, addictive sound, and then Bruce launches into an airy, pastoral, uplifting ballad where the metronomic feel allows you to escape the torpor induced at the beginning of the album. A musical surge, ambient with an encroaching synth, the album truly takes off with this sound reminiscent of PINEAPPLE THIEF, a return to their roots. "Stared Down" returns to its primal acoustic roots, its latent intimacy lingering on post-rock undertones, reminiscent of ANATHEMA, with that famous, soaring guitar solo."Kept Me Thinking," the creaking of a chair on the side of a house in Louisiana, is the first of two long tracks; I was getting impatient. Note the contribution of Jon, a PINEAPPLE THIEF collaborator, on bass for this crescendoing track that flows like a drink in the middle of the desert. Easy melody, vocals, and a melancholic guitar worthy of Brother CAVANAGH. A track that reminds us that you don't need a whole fleet of instruments to be great. The final solo screams with joy, lets loose, and feels good; an oriental-tinged choral finale. "Ghosts in the Park" begins with a meandering acoustic guitar, the other a plaintive electric ballad typical of PINEAPPLE THIEF?old habits die hard. A suspended 1'45" intro, and you think it's over; and then, and then the air begins to move, tickling our ears, leaving us to search for the musical direction, the Oberhausen creative space. The essence of the progressive spirit is evident in the minimalist drums accompanying these radiant post-acoustic guitar notes, letting the ear wander for a long time, taking its time. The finale seems to settle at the 10-minute mark, but then comes the organic shift, a fragile, latent sound, a musical spiderweb drawing the listener into Bruce's very room, listening to him strum and hum this last fleeting, archaic, ephemeral melody.Bruce Soord has given himself up without musical artifice; emotion, restraint, intimacy, and sincerity define this stripping bare with his acoustic guitar.

items.body: Review by alainPP — "The Silent Architect" features an organic rhythm followed by a groove worthy of Dream Theater, a metal riff with a "Kashmir-like" feel, and a melodic battleground. Nathan's voice dazzles over a heavy prog riff reminiscent of Kamelot, for example. The guitar solo and other solos drive the frenetic rhythm and instrumental onslaught, all power metal. "Doors of Yesterday" is a melancholic ballad highlighted by Dean's piano, with a saccharine classical orchestration over a pop melody oozing emotion, its metallic riff subtly present in the background. It evokes fond memories of the 80s, a time when quality reigned supreme. "The Invisible Countdown" boasts a distinctive vocal style, a reminiscent of Vanden Plas's prog metal DNA, and a wild, heavy riff. The catchy, mainstream heavy rock melody features a sharp guitar solo and an orchestration approaching the valiant Fates Warning. The final fade-out is somewhat redundant, however. "Mr. Crazy" breaks the mold, offering the raw, frenetic, and compulsive hard rock of their earlier work, with Nathan sounding more like Aerosmith. A punk-infused track with a colossal drumbeat, perfect for some serious headbanging. "Arrow" is the second, more mainstream, mid-tempo ballad, soothing on acoustic guitar and filled with backing vocals from Nathan and Dean. The irresistible melody makes you want to sing along to the chorus, shoulders intertwined; it's 80s rock boosted by today's powerful sound."Dust & Bone" kicks off again, like a heavy machine gun, the sharp rhythm throwing debris in all directions. A near-thrash track with a raw, swirling solo and a killer rhythm section?I stand by it; punchy and explosive. "Enemy In The Garden," the fourth full-length track, features a prog-metal intro that launches Nathan's restrained vocals over guest keyboardist Matt Guillory, James Labrie's regular keyboardist. As you might have guessed, the Dream Theater influence is evident, especially with the solemn break, the pounding pads, and the melting guitar. At one point, you might think you recognize a Pink Floyd vibe, and you wouldn't be wrong. It restarts, highlighting the contrast of this seemingly effortless piece with the excellent second guitar solo. The notes are even higher, and the interplay of vocals and instruments forges the album's standout track. "Ghost Hands," the third acoustic guitar ballad, is simple, effective, gentle, and enchanting. The fragile vocals evoke goosebumps, and the obligatory guitar solo sounds even better; impressively effortless. "Left In The Fire" boasts an intro-riff worthy of Metallica; The cinematic sound brings the power of the machine-gun riff, the keyboard in the background adds the richness to highlight the best notes. It's molten prog metal, resting in its blazing furnace, with Nathan delivering a beautiful vocal performance over a terrifying, savage, tribal rhythmic foundation. A sharp break, the beauty of the acoustic sound before Dean's fiery solo forges a new musical path. The epic arrives, the arpeggio dripping down, delivering the coup de gr�ce to this track. Nick's metronomic drumming guides the finale over the vocal-guitar chord before the delicate outro, a warm acoustic guitar solo, with Nathan's performance moving to the very end.TERAMAZE is back in the saddle after their previous album; here, it's a prog metal masterpiece, blending vocals, rhythm, riffs, edgy melodies, and warm ballads.(4.25)

items.body: Review by The Progolyte — This very obscure solo artist from Rome by the name of Stefano Testa only has a single album from the seventies under his belt, but I personally think it does more than you think. It's quite pretty, lacking in terms of that overall bombastic sound that I like in most of my Italian music, but still good enough to make an impact. And with an album cover like that, you can tell there's going to be something interesting in here. I think the overall performance could've been more exciting, but the laid-back and relaxed vibes of the material sort of fit well with the more singer-songwriter-oriented music on this record, especially in the second half of the album where the songs get short. Moving on to the personnel, it's Stefano Testa on piano, rhythm guitar, and vocals, and then his band that plays with him consists of Marco Coppi on flute, Alberto Monpellio on moog, Cosimo Fabiano on bass, Ottavio Corbellini on drums, and then Portici takes care of the rest of the guitars. My favorite track on here has to be the grand and thoroughly written sixteen-minute-long suite titled Una Vita. It has various different sections stitched together into one great composition, with mainly more dramatic acoustic bits but also taking use of almost spoken word passages and steady rock rhythms. It's really strong and shows a high level of craftsmanship but is admittedly a little slow and inconsistent in parts. You could say Stefano and the band could've had more enthusiasm in their playing, and though it is strong, it feels lacking when it comes to their overall energy. The rest of the songs are all quite short and uneventful, mainly being simple melodies with limited instrumentation. You can feel like it's going somewhere, but in the end it lies stagnant and doesn't evolve in the way you'd imagine. The highlights from this section were La Ballata Di Achab/Moby Dick and Il Dio Sulla Ferrovia, which had some interesting details such as more progressive structures and sections. In conclusion, this album sort of felt like a letdown, seeing how it had a rating of 4.06 at the time of writing this, but it's still generally an okay record. A bit lacking here and there, not bringing many original ideas to the table, but still a fun one if you like your Rock Progressivo Italiano fit with a lighter and simpler tone. This record will be getting a low 3.5/5.

items.body: Review by Dapper~Blueberries — Bye bye Scott Kelly! You abusive loser.Ok, that aside, me and Neurosis have been in a pretty comfy relationship. I am not the biggest fanof them in comparison to their contemporaries like Isis, or Cult of Luna, but their releases havealways left a pleasant taste in my mouth. So, when I heard they were making a new studio work, adecade after their last one from 2016, I figured it wouldn't hurt to review them. Right?No it didn't hurt. In fact, this record is actually really great! An Undying Love for a BurningWorld is genuinely really solid stuff that I wouldn't argue with anyone if they say this was one oftheir favorites from the band.Initially, I was a bit cautious considering that their previous works, while good, didn't leave muchof an impression on me. But I think two key factors made me change my mind and wish to really reviewthis one.For one, the new vocalist, Aaron Turner of Isis fame is incredibly good, and a great fit forNeurosis' sound. I was quite surprised that Aaron was willing to fill the slot of vocalist,especially considering Isis disbanding in 2010. But, honestly, who better to fill the void than fora fellow veteran of post metal to set the new standard for the future of this legendary band?Not only that, but his vocals are just superb as ever. Seriously, I say his voice aged like a finewine. His screams are poignant; His growls are superb. Seriously, why wasn't he in this band sooneris what I'm wondering?The second factor, though, is atmosphere. Not like previous Neurosis records couldn't have anoticeable vibe, but they weren't always their strong suit, even in the post metal space. Honestlythe only one that really stuck out to me was Souls at Zero. But An Undying Love for a Burning World?Hoo boy this thing is juicy with tension. The band still plays how they'd play years ago, but theyreally push themselves by really going noticeably away from sludge metal, and into horizons thatfeel like a heavier version of that of Godspeed You! Black Emperor, whilst also combining elementsfrom Isis, and Coil to really make it all work. It's genuinely such a vibe, and makes for somereally impressive music.The best track in this regard is easily Blind, in my opinion. This is probably the most post metalsong that has ever been post metal'd since Locust Star.Though, this record isn't perfect for me. Don't get me wrong, if this record was a person, I'd dateit, but at the same time it does suffer a tiny, minute, almost inconsequential problem that sort ofsours the pot, and that's Last Light, the big 16 minute track of the record. It's not a bad song,far from it. But at the same time, I feel like it doesn't quite END this record the best. You knowthat feeling you get when you have a show or series that you really, really like, and the lastepisode comes out and you aren't totally wowed by it? That's this song for me. It's definitely good,as it has a great middle with two decent beginnings and ends, but nothing that really screamsfinale, if anything.Heck, sometimes I get confused and think there is something more after it. But no. Honestly I thinkthe previous track of In The Waiting Hours would be a better end for this record. If they swappedthose around, than I think the record would be near perfect.Other than that, though, An Undying Love for a Burning World is certainly one of Neurosis' standoutrecords now, at least for me. It has depth, beauty, and heaviness galore that really makes me wantto see what they'll do next. Certainly a recommendation.Best tracks: First Red Rays, Blind

items.body: Review by Finnforest — A Most Welcome Reprieve Stumbling half-conscious through the wreckage of mid-80s Banco, one could be forgiven for despairwhile pondering what could possibly follow E Via, the 1985 album that many figured must bethe end of the progressive juggernaut, for real this time. After all, it made 90125 andGenesis Shapes seem like masterpiece-level material by comparison. E Via had hit melike the worst moments of Chicago 17 and Invisible Touch put through a blender. I felt ready to liedown and embrace the end when, out of absolute nowhere, arrives Donna Plautilla. I don't know who Donna is supposed to be historically, but to me she was an angel of mercy in thismoment of Banco's discog. While dropping in 1989, the archival material was actually recorded 20years earlier by the newly-formed Banco of the late '60s: the Nocenzi brothers, the Falco brothers,and Franco Pontecorvi. This is embryonic Banco music and, despite falling well short of the grandeurof their acclaimed 72-73 albums, it is nonetheless absolutely enjoyable proto-prog in the same veinas the first Yes album, From Genesis to Revelation, Ad Gloriam, and '60s Deep Purple.Yes, it is dated now and has a little bit of that '60s Iron Butterfly psych vibe and short songsformat that place it well short of something like Darwin, but even without Francesco DiGiacomo's vocal talent, one can still hear the beginnings of what might follow. The album is wellrecorded and mixed, so it sounds pretty fab considering the age and, at that point, unknown statureof the group. The tracks here are keyboard-led period rock that is slightly less adventurous than, say, the Yesdebut, but only slightly, and it quite nicely preludes the RPI movement that was soon coming.Without Di Giacomo in the fold at this point, the vocals are handled by Vittorio Nocenzi, and whilehe lacks the legendary Di Giacomo's pipes, the fact is that he does just fine. He's no slouch as asinger, and he has backing from the Falco brothers (who were from the band Crash). As you mightimagine, the songs have that certain Italian spice that informs the music, from the beautifullanguage to the all-too-brief classical guitar and flute and harpsichord moments. Otherwise thesongs are driven by great piano and organ runs backed by upbeat, grooving rhythm section. I love thebold and up-front bass by Fabrizio Falco. The songs may indeed be proto-prog, but they are neverboring or lacking enthusiasm. The tunes are engaging and well composed and not as dated in the "flowery sense" as otherpeer '60s "organ rock." Is this album going to change your world? Likely not, but it is a really nice gem for the Banco fangenerally, the chance to hear them in this developing stage and with good audio quality. Perhaps mypraise of this album is partially the result of being bludgeoned into near catatonic haze by EVia, with Donna by contrast coming across as some kind of manna from heaven due to myE Via waterboarding. I can't say. But I had a good time with Donna, whoever she was. Ihighly recommend this early glimpse of RPI for the sheer joy of the playing and obvious burgeoningcreativity. It's slam dunk 3 stars, and I'm right on the edge of going 4.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There's something both new and classic about Versailles... perhaps because it's from the '90s, but this French quartet could sound both symphonic and rock... with a touch of music hall, and beyond the very well-executed vocals in their original French, the instrumental sections were surprising, maintaining the intrigue without revealing the direction they would take. A certain urgency in the basic, somewhat mellow rock parts evaporated when passages typical of space rock arrived, with impressive Genesis-esque keyboard solos, all in the first of the album's three suites, Hybridite. Then came a distinctly Floydian section, with the bass and cosmic guitar alternating with the flute of Guillaume de la Piliere, their guitarist and singer.Brothers Benoit and Oliver de Gency on drums and bass respectively, along with Alain de Lille on keyboards, formed the core of this group that would produce three symphonic gems, the first of which is Don Giovanni. Erre au fil des �res, the second track, shines with mellotron and harpsichord, and the magnificent voice of Guillaume de la Piliere, who knows when to be dark and prophetic, or hopeful and celestial at other times. The complex guitar arrangements, sounding like cellos, and plucked bass lines with the mellotron in the background help create that dreamlike atmosphere, enhanced by the occasional whisper, the nuances of French chanson that run through your veins. Suddenly, a piano and flute emerge, and we see that there are ideas... there are melodies, there is execution, but there is also feeling, there is personality.Any trace of roughness seems to have been left in the past at this point, and complex arrangements and sophisticated sounds, as if we were at court, with guitars that ascend while the drums and keyboard accompany until the dramatic climax with the organ...which gives way to Don Giovanni, the central piece.There's a looseness in the bass, which at times gives the development a feel reminiscent of Yes, but when we least expect it, there's an almost chamber-like moment with flute and mellotron, with Guillaume singing and more elements that achieve that hybrid of cabaret and opera, in a context that then returns to the rock that ranges from King Crimson to Rush. Plus Alain de Lille's piano, which completely changes the mood, becoming classical in a fugue and leaving no symphonic corner unexplored... but feeling that they were not paying homage to anyone, but rather an original work, dedicated to Don Giovanni, whose imprint resonates deeply when the guitar is left alone and the whole band explodes for the grand finale.By the time we hear Subtiles D�licatesses...first solo with the harpsichord and then rocking out...Guillaume de la Piliere has become a new classic in his own right. Because he sings with such boldness, provocatively, with deep, high notes, and then the sharp guitar takes over...and then the other side with the harpsichord, with which he sings in unison.I'm not a fan of neo-progressive bands; I often demand originality from them and not copies of the classics of the past. That's why I usually stick to a few Norwegian ones, but this one really has something for me. There are influences, but "the tree doesn't obscure the forest," so to speak.Memoires D'H�catombes holds surprises, in addition to instrumental parts with pyrotechnic solos, then there will be variations with synthesizer solos in the style of Gong, of space rock...and a very operatic soprano voice floating in space only sustained by a rope, a thin rope of mellotron...to then close with bass and keyboard like a captivating whirlwind.Drama transcribes that operatic tension exposed throughout the album, with layers of keyboards like closing a curtain...a mantle of sober recollection after the exposed artificial lights, keys that like strings ascend...until they vanish in an echo that promises continuation.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — This version of Yes, with Jon Anderson singing so differently, so jazzy and psychedelic, already featuring Chris Squire, Bill Bruford, and Peter Banks with that variety of sounds... they would have stood out in the sea of ​​bands of the '60s even if they hadn't been the Yes we later knew. They weren't Beatles clones like so many others... and it was a different band, of course! Just listen to the acoustic ending of "Beyond and Before." And "I See You" is one of my favorite tracks... vocal harmonies in a jazzy, psychedelic context, Jon with a voice that sometimes sounded like many jazz singers at once, even Billie Holiday! Sometimes it's just the guitar and drums... and I think they were already a mature band of experienced musicians; in fact, several of them came from previous bands, and they only pale in comparison to their own future work... which was so different from what they were doing, despite the classical influences already present in Banks' solos.So what standard, what parameter to use? That of the progressive context? If so, the result would be uneven because some works were already pointing in that direction without even knowing it, while others, equally beautiful like Yesterday and Today, were more anchored in the 60s. Although that is precisely where the magic of this debut lies, its freshness, its variety...its honesty.Looking Around shows a mixed maturity, achieved in the instrumental aspect, in the execution, but not yet in the compositional aspect, where one could expect more originality in the arrangements, although the embryo of a more mature band is already present in The Yes Album years later.Harold Land displays an attempt at more complex, distinctly British composition, which, however, is light years away from the classic Yes style. Banks' guitar arrangements are impeccable, and Jon's voice is perfectly on point, emotive and epic... yet understated at the same time, which is what a song of this magnitude demands. "Every Little Thing" begins the final trio of tracks, which are also my favorites. When they stray from the script and Banks plays without following it, and Bruford follows him blindly, it's a different band, rawer, another good band with people we know, with nods to the Beatles that remain just that. And yet, the final result is uneven due to small details, such as unpredictable parts alongside others that are quite foreseeable and detract from the impact of the latter. In Sweetness you can enjoy Jon's clean and tender voice, Chris's bass, Paul Banks' guitar and Bill who could play with brushes or the edges like Brazilian bossa nova drummers, but it was still a little way off, you enjoy that previous experiment, which was definitely still a promise of what was to come...seemingly impossible to isolate oneself from the context...something that could be done with I see you.It goes without saying that Bill Bruford loves jazz... and Jon, throughout his career, has systematically returned to it like an old friend he may not see often, but whose affection remains undiminished. He has always demonstrated his attachment to the genre, whether on his second solo album, Song of Seven, or with the studio tracks on Keys to Ascension, or his collaboration with Jean-Luc Ponty a few years ago. This debut also speaks to that, and therein lies its value, beyond its level within the progressive standard.Survival has that unique magic of Swinging London...from that photo shoot with those statues in the album booklet...that makes it eternal, that never ages.

items.body: Cicadas does a beautiful job using an experimental musical lens to help focus our attention on an often overlooked yet fascinating creature who lives in a world completely different from ours, yet that is also exactly the same (a beautiful expression of German phenom​enological biologist Jakob von Uexküll’s concept of the Umwelt or life-world that is specific to the sensory perceptions of each kind of animal). Eerie liquid stringlike sounds lend a darker, horror film soundtrack feel Cicadas: Broods XIX and XIII by Robert Thurman   Groups of cicadas that emerge during the same year in the same North American region on a periodical cycle of 13 or 17 years are known as broods. In 2024 two broods emerged together—the Great Southern Brood known as XIX and the Northern Illinois Brood known as XIII–leading to a massive cicada bloom (or infestation, depending on your point of view) in the areas where the two broods overlapped. As part of his ongoing “Poetic Nature” series of artworks, poems, and musical compositions, Robert R. Thurman crafted Cicadas to memorialize this momentous combined emergence, the first in two centuries. For me Cicadas does a beautiful job using an experimental musical lens to help focus our attention on an often overlooked yet fascinating creature who lives in a world completely different from ours, yet that is also exactly the same (a beautiful expression of German phenom​enological biologist Jakob von Uexküll’s concept of the Umwelt or life-world that is specific to the sensory perceptions of each kind of animal). I love cicadas for their fantastic dinosaur/alien appearance—periodical cicada adults in the genus Magicicada have coal-black bulbous bodies, bright red eyes, orange-veined wings and legs that taper to black at their tips–and for their cascading susurrations of sound that mean summer has truly arrived to North Texas (for photos, recordings, and tons of scientific information you can visit the Periodical Cicada Info Pages. For many of us in the U.S. who grew up listening to annual cicadas (different species than the periodical ones, but similar vibe in sound and appearance) as kids lolling around through long, steamy summer days, their calls bring a certain nostalgia. This nostalgic feeling about summer cicadas is certainly shared by many in Japan judging from how often the calls of cicadas signal poignant moments of transition from youth to adulthood and longing for lost innocence in manga and anime. Thurman’s Cicadas consists of three long tracks, the first two clocking in at about ten minutes each, and the last at fourteen. The album begins with the appropriately named “Emergence.” Brushed, syncopated percussive elements do a great job evoking the unexpected emergence patterns of thousands of individual animals pushing their way to the surface of the soil at slightly different times. Repeated drones that arise later in the track feel a bit like sirens passing on a distant highway, making me think of the bright red eyes of these unnerving-looking creatures. Eerie liquid stringlike sounds lend a darker, horror film soundtrack feel. Periodic flickering and ringing resounds as cicadas buzz past your ears on their inscrutable errands, like busy travelers jostling one another in the airport as they speed their way along. Cicadas buzz past your ears on their inscrutable errands :: On “Aggregations” Thurman leans into the alien invader feel of cicada broods. The sounds here remind me a bit of ELTA Music’s Solar 42 analog drone machine that one of my students used this past semester to evoke a 1950s giant insect film for one of the segments of a cicada-focused soundwalk composition she created. Drones swell and ebb in waves, like male cicadas chorusing to attract females for mating on romantic sunlit treetop branches. Later in the track a phaser-like sound emerges, a laser-focusing beacon sent over the airwaves solely for female cicada listeners. At first the scale feels off-putting: nearly every open surface on each branch and tree-trunk covered with cicadas. But eventually the thick sounds start to feel more familiar and even reassuring, like the summer calls of more well-known annual cicadas. “Chorusing” sounds almost transcendent: a luminous quality resonating as males with their tymbal-scraping calls and females with their wing-flicks respond to each other, duetting in a language of love only their own kind fully understands, yet with an unearthly beauty this track helps all of us appreciate. The listener gets a clear feeling of many insect bodies packed closely together, wings vibrating in choruses of rising tides of excitement followed by calmer periods. By the end the track becomes much quieter as the chorus stills and the massive brood recedes for another 13 or 17 years. Cicadas: Broods XIX and XIII is available on Bandcamp. items.body: RL Huber of Eureka Springs, Arkansas has an orchestral sound, with abundant strings and pianos, and a classical-drone crossover feeling that is complex and subtle. Meditation drones elevated in some sunny mountains Sea Legs by RL Huber   RL Huber of Eureka Springs, Arkansas has an orchestral sound, with abundant strings and pianos, and a classical-drone crossover feeling that is complex and subtle. The title “Sea Legs” makes me think of learning to walk through the relentless bobbing motion on a boat in rough waters; contrast this with the sound here, which makes me think of meditation drones elevated in some sunny mountains, a classical ambient avant-garde terrestrial sojourn. It is all very curious and lovely, in a very peculiar way. The longer ambient composition has a sustained tone style, a slow series of long notes using what sounds like traditional classical string instruments. The entire orchestra focuses on one note that changes every few moments, slowly taking form, “Sea Legs” (9:17). Long silky drones that shift, now a piano emerges with the same concept, one note holds then another note comes along, the way that the notes change, the intervals are similar, creating the feeling of slow twilight music. “Slowly Traversing the Wall” (5:14) is a drone / field recording piece, I hear a slow gravelly hiss, a distant foghorn, wind. There could be a brief sustained piano note in the mix, perhaps a slow drone nocturne. The closing track, “Silt and Sand” (3:49) begins with a bit of distortion and wistfulness, nestled with beloved bowed tones. The song title suggests that we are on the beach, feeling the textures of the grains. “I have been recording experimental music since 2004 using project names such as Vopat, Olekranon and Sujo as well as my own name, Ryan Huber. I have recorded a number of albums in the electronic, noise and drone genres. Memories of Falling incorporates these elements with a more restrained approach. I have been influenced by modern artists such as John Cage, Tim Hecker and Anna Thorvaldsdottir.”There are nine RL Huber releases available on Bandcamp, including Sea Legs, Themisto, Glass House Architecture, Dagos, Hafgufa, Forgiving Light, Return of the Cosmonaut, Memories of Falling, and Animan Edere.Eureka Springs is a city in the Ozark Mountains of northwest Arkansas, known for the preserved Victorian buildings of its Historic District, such as the Palace Bath House, Basin Park Hotel and Crescent Hotel, all built around the city’s natural springs. In the nearby hills, soaring Thorncrown Chapel is a striking wood and glass church. To the south, Turpentine Creek Wildlife Refuge is home to big cats and bears. Sea Legs is available on Bandcamp. items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — The band released its sole album BIZITAKO GAUZEK (Things Lived) in 1978 on the Elkar label and citedthe big players in the English scene as the primary focal points for references. Pink Floyd, Yes,King Crimson, Genesis and even Emerson, Lake & Palmer provided the blueprints for which SAKREcrafted its own unique brand of symphonic rock and although the band is noted in history for beingone of the few to actually engage in a more rock oriented style of prog, BIZITAKO GAUZEK still findsmany moments of softer folky moments it's just that they are not derived from the band's own uniqueisolate heritage and therefore SAKRE was much closer to other Spanish and Italian symphonic progbands with romantic lead vocals, dreamy sweeping synthesizers, melodic guitar riffing, group vocalharmonies and theatrical concept based compositions.As one of the first prog bands to emerge after the fall of the Franco dictatorship, SAKRE honed itschops on the live circuit for years before recording its sole release. Taking on the truecharacteristics of a 70s prog band, SAKRE delivered a full blown dramatic concept album with emotivemovements that spanned ten tracks but sadly limited to a mere 34 minutes. The band has cited suchclassics as The Who's "Quadraphenia" and Genesis' "The Lamb That Lies Down On Broadway" as keyreferences for the subject matter which in this case tackles the psychological state of a person'slife and the trials and tribulations which sort of qualifies them as an early prototype of the worldof neo-prog which would soon adopt the same techniques and become the first official prog revivalgenre. Also like a great prog release this one is fortified with lots of bold time signatureworkouts, a trait eschewed by many of the mellow Basque folk crowds crafting more subtle versions ofprog folk.While the opening "Erreberentzia (Ohiko Dantza)" insinuates yet another dreamy folk album emergingfrom northeastern Spain with some traditional wind instrument and a ritualistic drum beat withoutany accompanying instrumentation, the following "Orain" quickly dispels those assumptions anddisplays a more symphonic rock approach with guitar-fueled riffing and the notable absence of anyflute sounds whatsoever. Tracks like "Ezengaino" fire on all prog cylinders with Squire-esque bassgrooves, beefy organ swells accompanied by Emerson keyboard wizardry and jazzy drum rolls punctuatedwith wily time signature off shoots courtesy of the early Yes years. The album loses no momentum asit continues delivering high quality tracks that culminate with the satisfying climactic closer"Bilatzea" leaving me to wish this album was a bit longer as there are really no stagnant moments tobe found. While perusing through the various Basque progressive acts that spanned a short period of just a fewyears, this band clearly stood out sounding nothing like Haizea, Izukaitz, Magdalena, Enbor and therest. Only Lisker engaged in a more rock oriented approach. This is an excellent album marred onlyby its rarity of only being available as a first print vinyl edition and of course that the conceptis unintelligible to all except native Basque speakers. Musically though this sounds most similar tomore guitar oriented symphonic prog bands from Italy given the rhythmic flow of it all even thoughthe English scene was cited as the key wellsprings of inspiration. All in all this is one of myfaves to emerge from the lesser known Basque scene which stood out of the homogenous pack like asore thumb but all the best for it.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — While the Rock Andaluz scene was hitting Spain full force by the mid-1970s, another daring group ofbold prog enthusiasts were also offering new strains of flamenco infused jazz fusion with the lion'sshare emerging from the Catalonian city of Barcelona. While Iceberg may be the best known of thesecrafty weavers of complexity, other acts such as Companyia El�ctrica Dharma, Orquestra Mirasol,Barcelona Traction and Secta S�nica were delivering their own wild fusion expressions. Add to thatanother band M�SICA URBANA which dropped two highly revered albums in its three year existence. Thisband was perhaps the most adventurous of the lot as it tackled not only a wide swath of fusionstyles laid down by the likes of Return To Forever, Mahavishnu Orchestra, Herbie Hancock and WeatherReport but also incorporated the crafty complexities of England's Canterbury scene and if thatwasn't enough wove intricate third stream classical elements as well as the homegrown folk flavorsof the region including the sounds of Andalusian flamenco.Some of the best musicians on the scene in this one included Joan Albert Amarg�s (keyboards, windinstruments), Carles Benavent (bass, later of Paco de Luc�a's band), Salvador Font (percussion),Llu�s Cabanach (guitars), and special guest Aurora Amarg�s (castanets). The band released itseponymously titled debut in 1976 and has been considered one of the highlights of Spain's entirefusion scene from the 1970s. The band was sort of a supergroup in a local sense and very much soundslike one at this point by delivering amazingly dexterous labyrinthine compositions that intricatelyintegrated jazz, progressive rock, classical music and traditional Spanish folk musical styles withthe intent of exuding a truly Iberian vibe without sounding derivative. Perhaps comparable only toArgentina's Alas as far as unbridled complexities are concerned, M�SICA URBANA delivered anunpredictable pastiche of musical ingenuity that few acts would dare attempt much less pull off withsuch ease and grace.The album wastes no time bedazzling the unsuspecting listener with its opening "Agost" with wilycurveball guitar riffs in cahoots with slinking keyboards slithering around in strange ways whilethe bombastic incessant shifts of tempos, time signatures and dynamics prove to be a difficult taskin keeping track of. In fact it's the equivalent to a musical roller coaster that does all thoseimpossibly crazy loops and hairpin turns into the unknown. It's a wild ride that rarely allowsmoments of respite however in the middle of the turbulent fusion-fests also exist moments of melodicmellowness however they usually don't last too long before explosive bursts of energetic excesspunctuate the serenity. It's a jittery beast of an album bar none which will surely alienate all butthe most hardened fusionists looking for the absolute pinnacle of no [%*!#]s to give fusion at itsmost unapologetically dynamically creative fortified with as many high octane ingredients aspossible. It's an exhilarating ride which provides both smatterings of melodic accessibility in themidst of impossible mangled motifs of madness.While many fusionists were adopting funk about this time to ease the pain of the wild torrents ofjazz infused curveballs, M�SICA URBANA took the opposite approach and indulged in a musical free-for-all where no limits were set however the band remains firmly in the world of jazz fusion as itsprimary modus operandi. The band would calm things down a bit for its second and final releasehaving realized that perhaps there weren't enough music nerds out there to sustain the marketabilityof an album like this debut however for those of you who resemble those remarks this is an amazinglybrilliant display of jazz fusion run amok. Spain was late to the game in regard to the most daringexpressions of prog and fusion due to political repression but once the flood gates were open thisfeisty nation proved it had the talent to compete with the best on the international scene andM�SICA URBANA stands as one of Spain's most exciting and enigmatic examples.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — Considered one of the pillars of the Rock Urbano scene in Spain, the Madrid based LE�O (means "log"of all things!) emerged from one of the progenitors of the style, �u in which founder and frontmanRosendo Mercado played guitar from 1974-77 before he butted heads with the notoriously difficultJose Carlos Molina and left before that band's debut "Cuentos De Ayer Y De Hoy" hit the market.While it would take a while to regroup, in 1978 the band was born and existed for five years untilthe Rock Urbano boom gave way to the increasing popularity of new wave and post-punk. Initiallyfeaturing Rosendo Mercado on guitar and vocals, Ramiro Penas on drums and Chiqui Mariscal on bass,Mariscal abruptly departed during the recording of the band's self-titled debut release and replacedby Tony Urbano. The power trio would remain intact for the rest of the band's existence. Due to someof the material being already recorded, both bassists appear on this debut release.The band's debut hit the scene in 1979 and featured a sound in the brackish waters where 70s progwas intertwined into a more contemporary hard rock / early heavy metal sound. One of thedistinguishing features of Rock Urbano was the use of the Spanish language in protest against theuniversal adoption of English as the lingua franca of the music industry. Spain was definitelyprotective of its indigenous features and this particular movement found a short burst of popularityaround the end of the 70s. LE�O's debut was a triumphant display of highly energetic melodic hardrock laced with raw guitar heft and crafty complex compositions that were reminiscent of similarlyminded acts from other nations such as Captain Beyond, Rush, Lucifer's Friend and Uriah Heep onlytaking things into even heavier territories threatening to launch the entire New Wave of BritishHeavy Metal Scene in the process.Consisting of seven tracks, this eponymous beginning featured extended prog-fueled instrumentalprowess in cahoots with vocal oriented hard rock heft and while the album in many ways exemplifies atypical heavier rock album of the late 70s. it is the unorthodox compositional approach that weavesunexpected tempo changes and labyrinthine journeys through certain longer tracks that keeps itplanted in the declining prog value system that had dominated the 70s but when this album wasreleased in 1979 finding a declining return value which is why the band would abandon these excesseson its sophomore album and jump on the more straightforward hard rock bandwagon. The album beginswith the sizzling guitar frenzy at the beginning of "Castigo" and remains fired up for most of its40 minute journey.While guitar riff churning is the usual modus operandi of LE�O's debut, slower more symphonic progmotifs do emerge such as on the atmospheric "La Nana" which is the most subdued track on board aswell as the acoustic guitar closer "Se Acab�!!!" which serves as a come down track from theadrenalized hard rock relentlessness that preceded. Considered a classic in the Spanish hard rockworld, LE�O unleashed an excellent slide of proggy hard rock on this cleverly crafted debut thatseems to pay tribute to the prog fueled 70s while recognizing the hard rock / heavy metal 80ssimultaneously. While the band's lyrics are exclusively in Spanish, the album is also notable forsocial criticism and other once taboo subject matter that were utterly banned before Franco's deathin 1975. It's definitely a hallmark of Spanish hard rock and sets itself apart from much of thegeneric competition. Very much in the vein of �u only without the Tull-ish flute and folk flavors.

items.body: Review by AFlowerKingCrimson — I'll admit I'm not a Supertramp expert or a hardcore fan of the band. I own all of their studio albums from Crime of the Century up to and including Breakfast in America. I'm ok with that for now. I also used to own (and maybe still have somewhere) the Famous Last Words album (on vinyl). For this particular album I much prefer the songs sung by by Roger Hodgson as opposed to Rick Davies. They seem catchier and more melodic to my ears. Not that the ones that Rick Davies sung are bad but compared to the ones where Hodgson sings they don't do much for me. Still as a whole this is a great album and next to Crime of the Century probably the best Supertramp album I know.The album starts out with "Just a little bit" which features acoustic guitar up front and was the big hit from the album. It was even covered by the Goo Goo Dolls in 2004 but I'm not that familiar with that version. The title track "even in the quietest moments" is another highlight and is sort of to this album what the title track to A Farewell to Kings is to that Rush album. Like that one this one also features acoustic guitar and while an important song not the epic on the album. "Babaji" is a great deep cut with spiritually influenced lyrics (I don't remember the details). The highlight of the album is the epic "Fool's Overture." It could be argued that this is the only track on the album that is "pure prog." I won't get into a debate about that except to say that's not really how I would frame it. That said, this closing track is certainly the most typical prog track and at 10:52 is the longest track on the album. It has a recurring theme which comes back later which is always a nice surprise. So overall, In The Quietest Moments is a classic album by Supertramp and one of their best. Not a perfect album for me but certainly not a bad place to start if you are new to the band (although I personally would probably recommend Crime of the Century). Definitely a 4 star album.

items.body: Review by yarstruly — Clicked 5, but really 4.5...4 is just too low.Elder is a band founded in Boston in 2005, but has been based in Berlin, Germany for several years now. Their seventh full-length solo album, "Through Zero", is set to be released on May 29, 2026. I want to thank Jadd from Blues Funeral records (the band's US label) and Austin Griswold of Secret Service PR agency for providing me with a review copy. As always, I receive no further compensation, and this is a cold listen. I always call it like I hear it.Elder are known for their Heavy Psych Prog style. I have all of their albums since the 3rd album "Lore" from 2015 in my library and a smattering of tracks from their earlier work and have enjoyed a number of their songs. When I saw the buzz surrounding this release, however, I knew I had to reach out for a review copy. The album's six tracks range from 5:49-10:48.The lineup is:- Nicholas DiSalvo / guitar, vocals, synthesizer- Michael Risberg / guitar, Rhodes piano, slide guitar- Jack Donovan / bass guitar- Georg Edert / drums, percussion Time to jump in!Track 1 - Sigil to Ruin (10:39)The song begins with some quiet tones that fade in and slowly build until the band fully kicks in at about 25 seconds with a quick tempo heavy rhythmic groove. The guitars and synth play a melodic line over the steady pulse. At 1:45 an odd meter riff takes over as the music's dynamic level eases off. The full band returns to lead in the first vocals at around 2:20. The midrange vocals are draped with reverb and delays that fit the mood of the song nicely. I like how the track is in no hurry, taking its time to develop different themes and moods. Excellent heavy riffage kicks in at around 4:10. A bridge segment follows. A new section begins at around 6:20, heralded by delays that are panned hard to both speakers, giving a "ping-pong" effect; very cool! Just after 7 minutes a synth part takes over joined by drums with odd meter shifts. The electric piano begins to build around it, followed by tasty, delayed guitars then vocal harmonies. Just before 9 minutes, the music shifts again to a guitar solo over a new rhythm bed. This is very heavy, yet warm and spacious. After a big riff gives a final punctuation, the song winds down with various effects for the final several seconds. Outstanding opener!Track 2 - Capture/Releae (8:48)A warm synth chord fades in to commence the song. Sequenced synth patterns create a rhythm that is matched by the rhythm section. The rhythm is syncopated making it difficult to pin down the meter. At around 2:15, the music takes a turn for the heavy! After a short verse there is an instrumental section with meter-shifts-a-plenty. I love the harmonized guitar lines between vocal phrases in the next verse. At around 4 minutes, a "tribal" drumbeat provides the foundation for a bridge. At around 4:40, an instrumental break with guitar harmonies takes over. There are lots of juicy bits in this track for sure. Wow, the section that starts around 6:20 is really rockin'! Great guitar playing over the smokin' rhythm section. There is a lot going on here, in a very good way! The riffs are very fast and energetic, with nice smooth sustained guitar harmonies on the top as we approach the song's conclusion. Excellent cut!Track 3 - Through Zero (9:06)Let's see what the title track brings to the table. An arpeggiated guitar riff with a flanger, starts us off here. Then some very complex heavy riffing takes over with the rhythm section laying down an equally complex foundation. These guys really put the ROCK in Prog Rock. The first verse brings things down a good bit with minimal accompaniment initially, that builds up as we go along, with drums and bass entering. A heavy instrumental section follows. They are reminding me of a less angry Tool quite a bit here. I like the alternating light/heavy sections. At 4:00 a new 5-8 groove takes over. At around 5:15, layered guitars and distant vocal harmonies enter. I get the impression that the vocals are meant more as another layer of the soundscape at times. They become more prominent soon after. At around 6:35 there are some brain-tickling panned sounds for a few seconds before the band comes back hard and heavy. These guys are great at layering instrumental parts and stacking them up. While there are occasional standout guitar solos, the focus is more on tight, complex, ensemble playing. They seamlessly shift from one riff to the next before there is a final resolving chord then a repeating synth phrase. Another fantastic track!Track 4 - Strata (10:48)The synth from "Through Zero" leads us into this one. A low-pitched guitar riff joins it then the rhythm section joins in along with shimmering clean guitar parts on the top. The vocals come in at around 1:30 with minimal accompaniment. The harmonic structure of the vocals is somewhat akin to Alice in Chains. At around 3:35 a new, quick tempo guitar part takes over, to be joined by the rest of the band. Damn these guys are tight on the guitar harmonies while the rhythm section navigates all of the rhythmic twists and turns. These arrangements get quite dense at times, yet all of the parts can be discerned. I like the new riffs at around 7:30. The guitar solo on this one is a bit flashier than on the previous tracks. Then there is a major rhythm shift on a dime at 8:00 that made my head spin! It's a more straight-forward rock beat here. Things then smooth out a little at around 9 minutes. Just before the ten-minute mark they take it down to a low drone. Spacey synth lines close out the amazing song and take us into?Track 5 - Sight Unseen (8:50)The mellow synth parts continue gradually joined by guitar lines and a slowly building drum beat. They are really holding back here. Just before the three-minute point, however, the band comes in with some accents, but not in an overly heavy way. They then get into a Pink Floyd-like groove, if slightly heavier. So far, no vocals have appeared and we are past the halfway point. At just after 5:20 they start rockin' hard with odd meter riffs. What a great slow-burn instrumental this is turning out to be. With about one minute remaining, a sound effect shifts to a more mellow conclusion to our musical journey. Holy crap! What a ride that was!Track 6 - Blighted Age (5:49)The closing track brings acoustic guitar to the sound for the first time on the album, blended with a clean electric line. The vocals are smooth and I believe there are some conga drums initially providing the beat. The song begins to subtly build up in the second verse. At 2:15 things come back down. Electric piano enters shortly thereafter. There are some beautiful soundscapes being built here. This is a nice change of pace track to conclude the album on a more mellow note. Well-done.OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:This is the third album I have reviewed in the past few days that is set to be released near the end of May; all three have been incredible! As noted earlier, this band isn't about being flashy and showcasing their individual talents, although there are some fleeting moments that tell me that they could do that if they chose to. Elder, as a band, show that they are committed to creating a collaborative sound, and they do it extremely well! This is making me want to go back and give some more attention to their earlier releases. Fans of Tool, heavier Rush and even heavier Porcupine Tree/Steven Wilson will likely really enjoy this album. I give it 4.5 out of 5 stars or 90%.
